title: How Much Does It Cost to Build an AI Agent in 2026?
excerpt: A transparent breakdown of what AI agents cost to build and run — from a $5k support agent to $100k+ multi-system deployments — and the factors that move the number more than anything else.
body:
Almost every AI conversation we have starts with the same question: what will this cost? It is the right question, and it deserves a better answer than "it depends". Here is how AI agent budgets actually break down in 2026, based on the patterns we see across engagements.

## The short answer

Most production AI agents land between **$10,000 and $60,000** to build, with running costs of a few hundred to a few thousand dollars a month. Simple, well-scoped agents sit at the low end. Agents that touch many internal systems, carry compliance requirements, or handle voice sit at the high end.

You will see freelancers quote $3k and consultancies quote $250k. Both are real quotes for very different scopes. The range below explains what actually moves the number.

## What you are paying for

An AI agent project has four cost centres:

1. **Discovery and design (15–25% of budget).** Mapping the workflow, deciding where the agent acts autonomously versus where a human approves, defining failure behaviour. Skipping this is the single most common cause of failed agent projects.
2. **Core build (40–55%).** The agent itself: prompts, tools, retrieval over your data, integrations with your CRM or ticketing system, evaluation harnesses.
3. **Integrations and edge cases (15–25%).** Connecting to the two or three systems that make the agent genuinely useful, and handling the awkward real-world inputs your team will immediately find.
4. **Testing, security review and launch (10–15%).** Red-teaming the agent, setting up monitoring, and training the humans who will supervise it.

## Four price tiers in practice

### Tier 1: Task agent — $5k–$15k

One job, one channel, clear success criteria. A support agent that answers questions from your knowledge base and escalates everything it cannot handle. An internal agent that drafts replies for human approval. Two to four weeks of work.

### Tier 2: Workflow agent — $15k–$40k

The agent does things, not just says things: creates tickets, updates records, processes refunds within limits, calls APIs across two or three systems. This tier needs real engineering around permissions, audit trails and failure handling. Four to eight weeks.

### Tier 3: Voice or multi-channel agent — $30k–$70k

Voice adds latency engineering, telephony integration, interruption handling and much harder testing. Phone-based agents that book appointments or qualify inbound leads typically land here. Six to ten weeks.

### Tier 4: Multi-agent systems — $60k–$150k+

Several specialised agents cooperating across departments, with human-in-the-loop checkpoints, compliance requirements and custom evaluation infrastructure. These are programmes, not projects, and they should start with a paid pilot from an earlier tier anyway.

## Running costs: the part people forget

Model API fees are usually the smallest line. For a mid-volume support agent expect **$50–$500/month** in inference costs depending on traffic and model choice.

The real running costs are:

- **Hosting and observability** — $50–$300/month for most deployments
- **Knowledge base maintenance** — whoever owns your content owns the agent's accuracy; budget a few hours a month
- **Iteration** — plan for a tuning phase in the first 90 days after launch; agents improve fast when someone watches their transcripts

A useful rule of thumb: budget roughly 15–20% of the build cost per year for maintenance and improvement.

## What moves the price more than anything else

**Data readiness.** If your knowledge is scattered across PDFs, inboxes and three people's heads, cleaning it up is a project before the project. Clients with organised documentation routinely pay half what clients without it pay for the same outcome.

**Integration count.** Each system the agent reads from or writes to adds scope. Two integrations is a normal build; six is a different conversation.

**Autonomy level.** An agent that drafts for human approval is dramatically cheaper to build safely than one that acts unilaterally. Start supervised; expand autonomy once the track record earns it.

**Quality bar.** A cheap and impressive demo is usually an expensive disappointment in production — we are regularly called in to rescue sub-$5k agent builds.

## How to get a real number for your case

Come to a first conversation with three things: the workflow you want to automate, roughly how many times it happens per month, and which systems hold the relevant data. With those, a competent studio can give you a scoped estimate in one call — and tell you honestly if an agent is the wrong tool.

We publish this because we would rather clients arrive informed. If you want a scoped estimate for your own use case, [book a free consultation](/book-a-call) — no deck required, just the three facts above.
